title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Imagine you run a website with a newsletter, and you want as many visitors as possible to sign up. On your landing page, you have a single “call to action” (CTA) — a short line of text that prompts visitors to subscribe. You’re currently testing two versions:

CTA A: “Sign up for our newsletter here!”
CTA B: “Stay up to date by signing up!”

Which one actually works better? Your gut feeling isn’t enough — you need data. That’s where an A/B test comes in.
In an A/B test, each visitor to your site is randomly assigned to see one of the two CTAs. By randomly splitting visitors into two groups, we ensure that any difference in sign-up rates between the groups can be attributed to the CTA itself, not to some other difference between the visitors. After collecting enough data, we compare the sign-up rates across the two groups and use statistical tools to decide whether any observed difference is real or just due to random chance.
In this post, we’ll walk through the key ideas from classical frequentist statistics that underpin a proper A/B test — using simulation to make each concept concrete and intuitive.

text:
Imagine you run a website with a newsletter, and you want as many visitors as possible to sign up. On your landing page, you have a single “call to action” (CTA) — a short line of text that prompts visitors to subscribe. You’re currently testing two versions:

CTA A: “Sign up for our newsletter here!”
CTA B: “Stay up to date by signing up!”

Which one actually works better? Your gut feeling isn’t enough — you need data. That’s where an A/B test comes in.
In an A/B test, each visitor to your site is randomly assigned to see one of the two CTAs. By randomly splitting visitors into two groups, we ensure that any difference in sign-up rates between the groups can be attributed to the CTA itself, not to some other difference between the visitors. After collecting enough data, we compare the sign-up rates across the two groups and use statistical tools to decide whether any observed difference is real or just due to random chance.
In this post, we’ll walk through the key ideas from classical frequentist statistics that underpin a proper A/B test — using simulation to make each concept concrete and intuitive.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
section: The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
text:
The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
To analyze our A/B test rigorously, we need to frame it as a formal statistical problem.
Each visitor to our site either signs up (outcome = 1) or doesn’t (outcome = 0). This binary outcome is naturally modeled as a draw from a Bernoulli distribution: a coin flip with some probability \(\pi\) of landing heads (signing up). Because the two CTAs might influence visitor behavior differently, we allow the sign-up probability to differ between groups:

Visitors who see CTA A have sign-up probability \(\pi_A\)
Visitors who see CTA B have sign-up probability \(\pi_B\)

The quantity we actually care about is the difference in sign-up rates:
\[\theta = \pi_A - \pi_B\]
If \(\theta > 0\), CTA A is better. If \(\theta < 0\), CTA B is better. If \(\theta = 0\), neither outperforms the other.
Of course, we never observe \(\pi_A\) or \(\pi_B\) directly — we only see the outcomes for the visitors in our experiment. So we estimate \(\theta\) using the difference in sample proportions:
\[\hat\theta = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B = \hat\pi_A - \hat\pi_B\]
where \(\bar{X}_A\) is the fraction of CTA A visitors who signed up, and \(\bar{X}_B\) is the same for CTA B. This estimator \(\hat\theta\) is the central object of our analysis. The rest of this post explores its statistical properties through simulation.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Simulating Data
In the real world, we would never know the true values of \(\pi_A\) and \(\pi_B\) — that’s precisely why we run the experiment. But for the purposes of this exercise, we get to play God: we’ll set the true parameters ourselves, run our statistical methods, and verify that they behave as theory predicts.
We’ll assume:
\[\pi_A = 0.22, \quad \pi_B = 0.18, \quad \theta = \pi_A - \pi_B = 0.04\]
So CTA A is genuinely better by 4 percentage points. We simulate 1,000 visitors per group — 2,000 observations total.


Code
np.random.seed(42)

pi_A = 0.22
pi_B = 0.18
n    = 1000

draws_A = np.random.binomial(1, pi_A, n)
draws_B = np.random.binomial(1, pi_B, n)

print(f"Sample proportion for CTA A : {draws_A.mean():.4f}  (true: {pi_A})")
print(f"Sample proportion for CTA B : {draws_B.mean():.4f}  (true: {pi_B})")
print(f"Estimated difference θ̂     : {draws_A.mean() - draws_B.mean():.4f}  (true: 0.04)")


Sample proportion for CTA A : 0.2160  (true: 0.22)
Sample proportion for CTA B : 0.1780  (true: 0.18)
Estimated difference θ̂     : 0.0380  (true: 0.04)


Our sample proportions are very close to the true values of 0.22 and 0.18 — a reassuring sign. But why can we trust them? That’s what the next section is about.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Law of Large Numbers
The Law of Large Numbers (LLN) tells us that as the sample size grows, the sample mean converges to the true population mean. In our setting, this means \(\hat\pi_A \to \pi_A\) and \(\hat\pi_B \to \pi_B\) as we collect more data — and therefore \(\hat\theta \to \theta\).
The LLN is the foundational reason we trust our estimator: given enough data, it will get arbitrarily close to the truth. But how much data is “enough”? The plot below makes this tangible.
We compute the element-wise difference between our CTA A and CTA B draws, then track the running (cumulative) average of those differences as we add one observation at a time.


Code
diffs       = draws_A - draws_B
running_avg = np.cumsum(diffs) / np.arange(1, n + 1)











With only a handful of observations, the running average swings wildly. But as the sample size grows, the noise dies down and the estimate settles close to the true value of 0.04 (the red dashed line). This is the LLN at work: more data means a more reliable estimate.
The practical takeaway for A/B testing is clear: small samples can be deeply misleading. If you had stopped at 50 visitors per group, you might have drawn completely wrong conclusions. Size matters.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Bootstrap Standard Errors
Knowing that our estimator \(\hat\theta\) is close to the truth on average is useful, but it raises a follow-up question: how close? A point estimate without a measure of uncertainty is incomplete. We need a confidence interval.
One elegant way to quantify the uncertainty in \(\hat\theta\) is the bootstrap. The idea: instead of deriving a formula for the variability of our estimator, we use the data itself to simulate what would happen if we ran the experiment many times.
Here’s the procedure:

From our 1,000 CTA A observations and 1,000 CTA B observations, draw a resample of size 1,000 with replacement from each group.
Compute \(\hat\theta^* = \bar{X}_A^* - \bar{X}_B^*\) on the resample.
Repeat 1,000 times. The standard deviation of the 1,000 bootstrapped \(\hat\theta^*\) values is our bootstrapped standard error.



Code
B = 1000
boot_estimates = np.empty(B)

for b in range(B):
    resample_A        = np.random.choice(draws_A, size=n, replace=True)
    resample_B        = np.random.choice(draws_B, size=n, replace=True)
    boot_estimates[b] = resample_A.mean() - resample_B.mean()

se_boot = boot_estimates.std()

# Analytical SE for difference in two independent Bernoulli proportions
pi_hat_A = draws_A.mean()
pi_hat_B = draws_B.mean()
se_analytical = np.sqrt(pi_hat_A * (1 - pi_hat_A) / n +
                        pi_hat_B * (1 - pi_hat_B) / n)

theta_hat = pi_hat_A - pi_hat_B
ci_lower  = theta_hat - 1.96 * se_boot
ci_upper  = theta_hat + 1.96 * se_boot

print(f"Point estimate (θ̂)          : {theta_hat:.4f}")
print(f"Bootstrapped standard error  : {se_boot:.4f}")
print(f"Analytical standard error    : {se_analytical:.4f}")
print(f"95% Confidence interval      : [{ci_lower:.4f}, {ci_upper:.4f}]")


Point estimate (θ̂)          : 0.0380
Bootstrapped standard error  : 0.0177
Analytical standard error    : 0.0178
95% Confidence interval      : [0.0034, 0.0726]


The bootstrapped and analytical standard errors are very close to each other — the bootstrap “discovers” the right answer without needing a formula, purely from the data.
Our 95% confidence interval says: given our data, we estimate that CTA A’s sign-up rate exceeds CTA B’s by somewhere between 0.3% and 7.3% — a range that lies entirely above zero. This is strong evidence that CTA A genuinely outperforms CTA B.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Central Limit Theorem
The bootstrap gave us a practical tool for computing standard errors, but there’s a deeper theoretical result underpinning our ability to do inference: the Central Limit Theorem (CLT).
The CLT states that regardless of the shape of the underlying population distribution, the sampling distribution of the sample mean becomes approximately Normal as the sample size grows. In our case, even though individual outcomes are Bernoulli (binary 0/1), the distribution of \(\hat\theta = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B\) will look like a bell curve for large enough \(n\).
To see this in action, we simulate 1,000 experiments at four different sample sizes — \(n \in \{25, 50, 100, 500\}\) — and plot the distribution of \(\hat\theta\) each time.


Code
sample_sizes = [25, 50, 100, 500]
n_sim        = 1000

clt_results = {}
for ns in sample_sizes:
    theta_hats = np.array([
        np.random.binomial(1, pi_A, ns).mean() - np.random.binomial(1, pi_B, ns).mean()
        for _ in range(n_sim)
    ])
    clt_results[ns] = theta_hats











The progression is striking. At \(n = 25\), the histogram is jagged and irregular. By \(n = 100\), a clear bell shape is emerging. At \(n = 500\), the distribution is smooth and symmetric around the true value of 0.04. This is the CLT in action — and it’s why serious A/B tests require hundreds of observations per group, not dozens.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Hypothesis Testing
Now that we’ve seen the CLT in action, we can use it to run a formal hypothesis test.
We set up two competing hypotheses:

Null hypothesis \(H_0\): \(\theta = 0\) (the two CTAs produce identical sign-up rates)
Alternative hypothesis \(H_1\): \(\theta \neq 0\) (the CTAs differ)

The goal is to assess whether the data provide enough evidence to reject \(H_0\). We do this by standardizing \(\hat\theta\) to form a test statistic:
\[z = \frac{\hat\theta - 0}{SE(\hat\theta)}\]
The logic: by the CLT, \(\hat\theta\) is approximately Normal for large samples. Under \(H_0\), its mean is 0. Dividing by the standard deviation gives a standard Normal \(N(0,1)\) — whose distribution we know exactly, allowing us to compute a p-value.
A note on terminology: this is sometimes called a t-test, but strictly speaking that label applies when data are drawn from a Normal distribution. Our data are Bernoulli, so the CLT gives us approximate Normality — making this more accurately a z-test. For large samples the distinction is negligible.


Code
z_stat  = theta_hat / se_analytical
p_value = 2 * stats.norm.sf(abs(z_stat))

print(f"Estimated difference (θ̂) : {theta_hat:.4f}")
print(f"Standard error            : {se_analytical:.4f}")
print(f"z-statistic               : {z_stat:.3f}")
print(f"p-value                   : {p_value:.4f}")


Estimated difference (θ̂) : 0.0380
Standard error            : 0.0178
z-statistic               : 2.139
p-value                   : 0.0325


With a p-value well below 0.05, we have strong evidence against \(H_0\). If the two CTAs were truly identical, there would be only a tiny chance of observing a difference as large as ours by chance alone. We reject \(H_0\) and conclude that CTA A significantly outperforms CTA B.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The T-Test as a Regression
Here’s a surprising and useful fact: the two-sample test we just ran is mathematically equivalent to a simple linear regression.
We stack our data into a single dataset with:

\(Y_i\): the outcome (1 = signed up, 0 = didn’t)
\(D_i\): an indicator for CTA (1 = CTA A, 0 = CTA B)

And fit:
\[Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \varepsilon_i\]
The interpretation is clean:

\(\beta_0 = E[Y_i \mid D_i = 0] = \pi_B\) — the CTA B sign-up rate
\(\beta_0 + \beta_1 = E[Y_i \mid D_i = 1] = \pi_A\) — the CTA A sign-up rate
Therefore \(\beta_1 = \pi_A - \pi_B = \theta\), and \(\hat\beta_1\) is numerically identical to \(\hat\theta\)



Code
Y = np.concatenate([draws_A, draws_B])
D = np.concatenate([np.ones(n), np.zeros(n)])
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(2 * n), D])

beta      = np.linalg.lstsq(X, Y, rcond=None)[0]
beta0, beta1 = beta

residuals = Y - X @ beta
sigma2    = residuals @ residuals / (2 * n - 2)
cov_beta  = sigma2 * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)
se_beta1  = np.sqrt(cov_beta[1, 1])
t_stat_reg = beta1 / se_beta1
p_val_reg  = 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t_stat_reg), df=2 * n - 2)

print(f"β̂₀ (CTA B mean)  : {beta0:.4f}   (true π_B = 0.18)")
print(f"β̂₁ (difference)  : {beta1:.4f}   (matches θ̂ = {theta_hat:.4f})")
print(f"SE(β̂₁)           : {se_beta1:.4f}")
print(f"t-statistic       : {t_stat_reg:.3f}")
print(f"p-value           : {p_val_reg:.4f}")


β̂₀ (CTA B mean)  : 0.1780   (true π_B = 0.18)
β̂₁ (difference)  : 0.0380   (matches θ̂ = 0.0380)
SE(β̂₁)           : 0.0178
t-statistic       : 2.138
p-value           : 0.0327


The regression coefficient \(\hat\beta_1\) matches our earlier \(\hat\theta\) exactly, and the p-values agree closely. A minor difference in the standard error arises because OLS assumes a pooled variance across groups — for large samples this distinction is negligible.
Why does this equivalence matter? Because the regression framework generalizes naturally. Add covariates to control for user characteristics, add indicator variables to test more than two CTAs, or add interaction terms to check whether effects differ across devices. The t-test is a special case of regression, and understanding this connection unlocks a much more powerful toolkit.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Problem with Peeking
Your boss is impatient. She doesn’t want to wait until all 1,000 visitors per group have been observed. Instead, she wants to run the hypothesis test after every 100 visitors — peeking at \(n = 100, 200, \ldots, 1000\) — and stop early if any peek is significant.
This sounds reasonable. It’s not.
Each test at \(\alpha = 0.05\) carries a 5% false positive rate. When you run 10 such tests on accumulating data, you get 10 chances to make a mistake. The overall probability of at least one false rejection climbs well above 5%.
To see exactly how bad the situation is, we simulate 10,000 experiments in a world where the null is true: \(\pi_A = \pi_B = 0.20\), so any “significant” result is a false positive.


Code
np.random.seed(123)

n_experiments   = 10_000
peeks           = np.arange(100, 1001, 100)
false_positives = 0

for _ in range(n_experiments):
    A = np.random.binomial(1, 0.20, 1000)
    B = np.random.binomial(1, 0.20, 1000)

    for peek in peeks:
        a_sub = A[:peek]
        b_sub = B[:peek]
        p_a   = a_sub.mean()
        p_b   = b_sub.mean()
        se_p  = np.sqrt(p_a * (1 - p_a) / peek + p_b * (1 - p_b) / peek)
        if se_p == 0:
            continue
        z    = (p_a - p_b) / se_p
        pval = 2 * stats.norm.sf(abs(z))
        if pval < 0.05:
            false_positives += 1
            break

empirical_fpr = false_positives / n_experiments
print(f"Nominal false positive rate (single test) : 5.0%")
print(f"Empirical false positive rate (peeking)   : {empirical_fpr*100:.1f}%")


Nominal false positive rate (single test) : 5.0%
Empirical false positive rate (peeking)   : 19.9%


The empirical false positive rate balloons to around 19.9% — far above the nominal 5%. In other words, even when there is truly no difference between the CTAs, we’d incorrectly declare a winner in roughly one out of every four or five experiments.
This is why pre-registration matters in A/B testing: decide your sample size before collecting data, run the test once at the end, and commit to that result. If you want the flexibility to stop early, you need more sophisticated methods — such as sequential testing or Bayesian approaches — that properly account for the multiple looks. Classical frequentist tests applied naively with repeated peeking will mislead you far more often than you think.

title: Does Blueprinty’s Software Actually Help You Get Patents?
section: The Setup: A Question Worth ~$1 Million
text:
The Setup: A Question Worth ~$1 Million
Blueprinty sells software to engineering firms — tools purpose-built for drafting patent applications. Their marketing team wants to make a bold claim: firms that use our software win more patents.
It’s a compelling pitch. But is it true?
To find out, Blueprinty assembled a dataset of 1,500 mature engineering firms, tracking:

How many patents each firm was awarded over five years
Whether the firm uses Blueprinty’s software
The firm’s age (years since incorporation)
Its US region (Northeast, Midwest, South, Southwest, Northwest)

On the surface, you might think: just compare average patent counts between customers and non-customers. If customers win more patents, claim confirmed.
But that would be wrong — or at least, dangerously incomplete. Blueprinty’s customers are not a random sample of engineering firms. Firms that seek out specialized patent software are probably already more serious about IP strategy. They may be older, more established, or concentrated in tech-heavy regions. Any raw difference in patent counts could be driven entirely by those pre-existing differences — not the software itself.
This is the fundamental challenge of observational causal inference: the treatment (software adoption) isn’t randomly assigned, so we need a model. We’ll use Poisson regression estimated via Maximum Likelihood to isolate the software effect while controlling for age and region.

Patent Counts: Customers vs. Non-Customers









The raw numbers already tell an interesting story: customers average 4.13 patents versus 3.47 for non-customers — a gap of about 0.66. Before getting excited, we need to ask whether this difference might simply reflect who chooses to become a customer.


Are Customers Different to Begin With?

Regional Distribution









This is striking. Nearly 68% of Blueprinty’s customers are based in the Northeast, compared to just 27% of non-customers. The Northeast is the US epicenter of biotech, pharma, and advanced manufacturing — industries with aggressive patent strategies. If Northeast firms happen to patent more regardless of software use, our raw comparison would be badly confounded.


Firm Age









Firm age differences are modest (customers average ~26.9 years vs. 26.1 for non-customers), but the relationship between firm age and patents is probably non-linear. Including \(\text{age}^2\) in the regression lets the model capture a hump-shaped pattern — peak patenting in middle age, tapering off at the extremes.
The bottom line: customers and non-customers differ systematically on region. Without controlling for this, we’d be conflating the software effect with the “type of firm that buys software” effect. Regression is our tool for separating them.

title: Does Blueprinty’s Software Actually Help You Get Patents?
section: A Simple Poisson Model via Maximum Likelihood
text:
A Simple Poisson Model via Maximum Likelihood

Why Poisson?
Patent counts are non-negative integers: 0, 1, 2, … The Normal distribution is a poor fit — it’s continuous, symmetric, and places probability mass on negative numbers. The Poisson distribution is the natural starting point:
\[
f(Y \mid \lambda) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\,\lambda^{Y}}{Y!}, \qquad Y = 0, 1, 2, \ldots
\]
The single parameter \(\lambda > 0\) serves as both the mean and variance. We estimate it from data using Maximum Likelihood.


Deriving the Log-Likelihood
Given \(n\) independent observations \(Y_1, \ldots, Y_n\), the joint likelihood is:
\[
L(\lambda) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{e^{-\lambda}\,\lambda^{Y_i}}{Y_i!}
= e^{-n\lambda}\,\lambda^{\sum Y_i} \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{Y_i!}
\]
Taking the log:
\[
\ell(\lambda) = -n\lambda + \left(\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i\right)\ln\lambda - \sum_{i=1}^n \ln(Y_i!)
\]
The last term is constant in \(\lambda\). Setting \(d\ell/d\lambda = 0\):
\[
-n + \frac{\sum Y_i}{\lambda} = 0
\implies \hat\lambda_{\text{MLE}} = \bar{Y}
\]
The MLE is the sample mean — satisfying because the Poisson mean is \(\lambda\).


Coding and Plotting the Log-Likelihood


Show code
def poisson_loglikelihood(lam, Y):
    if lam <= 0:
        return -np.inf
    return -len(Y) * lam + np.sum(Y) * np.log(lam) - np.sum(gammaln(Y + 1))

Y_obs = df["patents"].values




Show code
lambda_grid = np.linspace(2.5, 5.0, 500)
ll_vals     = [poisson_loglikelihood(l, Y_obs) for l in lambda_grid]
ybar        = Y_obs.mean()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.5))
fig.patch.set_facecolor(C_BG)

ax.plot(lambda_grid, ll_vals, color=C_BLUE, linewidth=2.2, zorder=3)
ax.axvline(ybar, color=C_RED, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5, zorder=4)
ax.scatter([ybar], [poisson_loglikelihood(ybar, Y_obs)],
           color=C_RED, s=80, zorder=5)
ax.annotate(f"MLE = $\\bar{{Y}}$ = {ybar:.4f}",
            xy=(ybar, poisson_loglikelihood(ybar, Y_obs)),
            xytext=(ybar + 0.18, poisson_loglikelihood(ybar, Y_obs) - 500),
            fontsize=10.5, color=C_RED, fontweight="bold",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=C_RED, lw=1.2))

    title="Log-Likelihood of the Poisson Model",
    subtitle="Each firm treated as an iid draw from Poisson(λ)",
    xlabel="λ", ylabel="ℓ(λ)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









The curve has a single, well-defined peak. The dashed red line marks \(\hat\lambda = \bar{Y} = 3.685\), confirming the analytic derivation. To read the MLE off the plot visually, simply find the \(\lambda\) value at the highest point of the curve.


Numerical Confirmation


Show code
result = optimize.minimize_scalar(
    lambda l: -poisson_loglikelihood(l, Y_obs),
    bounds=(0.01, 20), method="bounded"
)
print(f"Sample mean   : {ybar:.6f}")
print(f"Numerical MLE : {result.x:.6f}")
print(f"Difference    : {abs(ybar - result.x):.2e}")


Sample mean   : 3.684667
Numerical MLE : 3.684667
Difference    : 1.28e-07


The optimizer recovers the sample mean to within floating-point rounding error — exactly as the calculus predicts.

title: Does Blueprinty’s Software Actually Help You Get Patents?
text:
Poisson Regression

From One \(\lambda\) to Many
The simple model assumed every firm shares the same patent rate. Poisson regression lets \(\lambda\) vary across firms:
\[
Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i), \qquad \lambda_i = \exp(X_i'\beta)
\]
Why \(\exp(\cdot)\)? Because \(\lambda_i\) must be positive, but \(X_i'\beta\) can be any real number. The exponential maps the real line to the positive reals and makes the model multiplicative: each unit increase in a covariate multiplies \(\lambda_i\) by \(e^{\beta_j}\).


Updating the Log-Likelihood


Show code
def poisson_regression_loglikelihood(beta, Y, X):
    lam = np.exp(X @ beta)
    return np.sum(-lam + Y * np.log(lam) - gammaln(Y + 1))




Building the Design Matrix


Show code
# Midwest is the reference region (dropped to avoid perfect collinearity)
regions_to_include = ["Northeast", "Northwest", "South", "Southwest"]

X_df = pd.DataFrame({"const": 1.0, "age": df["age"], "age_sq": df["age"]**2})
for r in regions_to_include:
    X_df[f"region_{r}"] = (df["region"] == r).astype(float)
X_df["iscustomer"] = df["iscustomer"].astype(float)

X_mat = X_df.values
Y_vec = df["patents"].values

print(f"Design matrix: {X_mat.shape[0]} rows × {X_mat.shape[1]} cols")
print("Columns:", list(X_df.columns))

title: Does Blueprinty’s Software Actually Help You Get Patents?
text:
The Effect of Blueprinty’s Software
A Poisson regression coefficient isn’t an “extra patents” number — the model is multiplicative and the effect size depends on each firm’s other characteristics. To get an interpretable answer we use the Average Marginal Effect approach:

Set every firm’s iscustomer = 0 → predict \(\hat{y}_0\)
Set every firm’s iscustomer = 1 → predict \(\hat{y}_1\)
Average \(\hat{y}_1 - \hat{y}_0\)



Show code
X0 = X_mat.copy(); X0[:, -1] = 0
X1 = X_mat.copy(); X1[:, -1] = 1

yhat_1 = np.exp(X1 @ beta_glm)
avg_effect = np.mean(yhat_1 - yhat_0)

print(f"Mean predicted patents (customer):     {yhat_1.mean():.4f}")
print(f"Average marginal effect of software:   +{avg_effect:.4f} patents")
print(f"As % of sample mean:                   +{avg_effect/Y_vec.mean()*100:.1f}%")

Mean predicted patents (customer):     4.2290

The headline number: using Blueprinty’s software is associated with approximately 0.79 additional patents over a 5-year period, holding firm age and region constant. Against a sample mean of ~3.7 patents, that’s a roughly 22% uplift — a real, meaningful difference.

title: Does Blueprinty’s Software Actually Help You Get Patents?
section: Conclusion: What We Can and Cannot Claim
text:
Conclusion: What We Can and Cannot Claim
The Poisson regression tells a coherent, statistically significant story: after controlling for firm age and regional location, Blueprinty customers receive more patents than comparable non-customer firms.
What this analysis establishes:

The patent gap persists after controlling for the Northeast concentration of customers and differences in firm maturity
The software effect is statistically robust and economically meaningful (~0.79 patents per firm over 5 years)
The model is internally consistent: numerical MLE equals the sample mean; BFGS and statsmodels GLM give nearly identical coefficients

What it does not establish:
This is an observational study, not a randomized experiment. We cannot rule out unobserved confounders — characteristics that simultaneously predict software adoption and patent success. Firms with dedicated IP teams might both adopt specialized software and file higher-quality applications. To definitively establish causality, you’d want a randomized trial or a richer set of firm-level controls.
The honest version of Blueprinty’s pitch: our customers win more patents, and that pattern holds up after controlling for firm age and region. That’s already a strong result — and it’s one this data can actually support.

title: Does Price Matter in Charitable Giving? Replicating Karlan & List (2007)
text:
Every year, Americans donate more than 2% of GDP to charitable causes, with over 89% of households giving to at least one organization. Yet despite the scale of this market, fundraisers have long relied on intuition rather than evidence. One of the most widespread beliefs in the industry is that larger matching ratios are more powerful: a “$3 for every $1 you give” offer is assumed to be far more compelling than a simple 1:1 match.
Dean Karlan and John A. List put this assumption to a rigorous test in their 2007 American Economic Review paper, “Does Price Matter in Charitable Giving? Evidence from a Large-Scale Natural Field Experiment.”
What is the “price” of charitable giving? When a leadership donor offers to match contributions at a 2:1 ratio, a donor effectively pays $1 to deliver $3 to the charity — the implicit price of providing $1 of the public good falls from $1.00 to $0.33. Standard economic theory predicts that lower prices increase demand, so higher match ratios should increase donations.
To test this, the authors partnered with a U.S. liberal nonprofit and mailed solicitation letters to 50,083 prior donors in August 2005. Individuals were randomly assigned to either a control group (no match offer) or one of several treatment conditions varying along three dimensions: the match ratio (1:1, 2:1, or 3:1), the maximum size of the matching fund ($25K, $50K, $100K, or unstated), and the suggested donation amount.
The results were striking — and largely contrary to fundraising conventional wisdom:

Matching works: the match offer increased the response rate by about 22% and revenue per solicitation by roughly 19% compared to the control group.
But larger ratios do not help: the 2:1 and 3:1 treatments produced virtually identical results to the 1:1 treatment — the difference in match ratio had no statistically significant effect.
Political context matters: the match effect appears to be driven mainly by donors in states that voted for George W. Bush in 2004, with little evidence of an effect in blue states.

These findings suggest that securing a larger match ratio may not be the most efficient use of fundraising resources. The mere existence of a match — not its size — appears to be what moves donors.
In the sections below, we replicate the paper’s key findings using the publicly available dataset. We reproduce Table 1 (balance checks confirming successful randomization), Table 2A Panel A (the main treatment effects on response rate and donation amount), and Table 3 Column 1 (the regression estimates of the match effect on the probability of giving). We also extend the paper’s results by visualizing the red/blue state heterogeneity, which the authors present only in tabular form.

title: Does Price Matter in Charitable Giving? Replicating Karlan & List (2007)
text:
Conclusion
Karlan & List (2007) deliver two counter-intuitive but robust results. First, matching grants work: merely announcing that a leadership donor will match contributions raises response rates and revenue per solicitation. Second, and more surprisingly, the size of the match ratio appears not to matter — donors respond just as strongly to a 1:1 match as to a 3:1 match.
Our replication closely reproduces the paper’s key numbers. The balance checks confirm the randomization was successful. Table 2A shows the response rate rising from 1.8% in the control group to 2.2% in the treatment group, with the three ratio sub-groups remaining indistinguishable from one another. The OLS regression in Table 3 recovers a treatment coefficient of 0.004, significant at the 1% level, with the ratio interaction terms close to zero and insignificant.
The additional visualization makes the red/blue state heterogeneity tangible: the aggregate match effect appears to be driven mainly by red-state donors, with little evidence of an effect in blue states. This suggests charitable giving is shaped not only by the price of the public good, but also by social identity and political context — a finding with broad implications for how organizations design and target their fundraising campaigns.

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
MaxDiff (also called Best-Worst Scaling) is a survey method for measuring the strength of people’s preferences across a set of items. In each screen, respondents see a small subset of all items — four in this study — and choose the one they like most and the one they like least. Repeating this across many screens allows us to infer the relative preference for each item from the pattern of choices.
The key advantage of MaxDiff over simple rating scales is that it forces genuine trade-offs. Rating scales suffer from scale-use bias — some respondents habitually give high scores, others cluster around the midpoint — making cross-respondent comparisons unreliable. MaxDiff eliminates this by requiring relative judgments, which tend to be both more reliable and more informative.
In this assignment, the ten items are the core courses in the UCSD Rady MSBA program. The goal is to estimate student preferences using three methods and compare them:

Counts Analysis — a simple score: percentage of times an item was picked best minus percentage of times picked worst
MNL via MLE — a multinomial logit model fit by maximizing the log-likelihood, yielding point estimates and standard errors
MNL via Bayesian MCMC — the same model fit with a Metropolis-Hastings sampler, yielding a full posterior distribution over the parameters

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
MaxDiff (also called Best-Worst Scaling) is a survey method for measuring the strength of people’s preferences across a set of items. In each screen, respondents see a small subset of all items — four in this study — and choose the one they like most and the one they like least. Repeating this across many screens allows us to infer the relative preference for each item from the pattern of choices.
The key advantage of MaxDiff over simple rating scales is that it forces genuine trade-offs. Rating scales suffer from scale-use bias — some respondents habitually give high scores, others cluster around the midpoint — making cross-respondent comparisons unreliable. MaxDiff eliminates this by requiring relative judgments, which tend to be both more reliable and more informative.
In this assignment, the ten items are the core courses in the UCSD Rady MSBA program. The goal is to estimate student preferences using three methods and compare them:

Counts Analysis — a simple score: percentage of times an item was picked best minus percentage of times picked worst
MNL via MLE — a multinomial logit model fit by maximizing the log-likelihood, yielding point estimates and standard errors
MNL via Bayesian MCMC — the same model fit with a Metropolis-Hastings sampler, yielding a full posterior distribution over the parameters

We expect all three methods to agree strongly at the top and bottom of the ranking. The primary advantage of the Bayesian approach over MLE is that uncertainty on derived quantities like preference shares can be read directly from the posterior samples, without approximation.

The counts analysis is the simplest approach. For each item \(j\), we compute the percentage of times it was picked as best (out of the number of times it was shown) and the percentage of times it was picked as worst. The score is the difference:

section: From MaxDiff Data to MNL Choices
text:
From MaxDiff Data to MNL Choices
Before fitting an MNL model, we need to understand how MaxDiff survey data converts into MNL choice observations (following the week-5 conjoint/MNL slides).
The MNL model assigns each item \(j\) a utility coefficient \(\beta_j\). On a task showing items \(\{a, b, c, d\}\), the probability that item \(b\) is picked best is the softmax over all four utilities:
\[
P(\text{best} = b) = \frac{\exp(\beta_b)}{\exp(\beta_a) + \exp(\beta_b) + \exp(\beta_c) + \exp(\beta_d)}
\]
The probability that item \(c\) is then picked worst — from the remaining three items — is equivalent to choosing the item with the lowest utility from that set. Flipping the sign of each utility and applying softmax gives:
\[
P(\text{worst} = c \mid \text{best} = b) = \frac{\exp(-\beta_c)}{\exp(-\beta_a) + \exp(-\beta_c) + \exp(-\beta_d)}
\]
Each task therefore yields two MNL observations: a best-pick from all four items, and a worst-pick from the remaining three.
Identifiability. Because the softmax is invariant to adding a constant to every utility, only relative utilities are identified. With 10 total items, we estimate 9 free parameters and fix \(\beta_1 = 0\) (AI Math, Item 1) as the reference category. All other coefficients are interpreted relative to AI Math.

MNL via Maximum Likelihood
The log-likelihood sums over all tasks:
\[
\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \sum_{\text{tasks}} \left[ \beta_{j^*_b} - \log\!\!\sum_{j \in \text{shown}}\!\!\exp(\beta_j) \;\;-\;\; \beta_{j^*_w} - \log\!\!\!\!\sum_{j \in \text{shown} \setminus \{j^*_b\}}\!\!\!\!\exp(-\beta_j) \right]

where \(j^*_b\) is the best-picked item and \(j^*_w\) is the worst-picked item in each task. We use the log-sum-exp form throughout for numerical stability.

def numerical_hessian(f, x, eps=1e-4):
    n = len(x)
    H = np.zeros((n, n))
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i, n):
            xpp = x.copy(); xpp[i] += eps; xpp[j] += eps
            xpm = x.copy(); xpm[i] += eps; xpm[j] -= eps
            xmp = x.copy(); xmp[i] -= eps; xmp[j] += eps
            xmm = x.copy(); xmm[i] -= eps; xmm[j] -= eps
            H[i, j] = (f(xpp) - f(xpm) - f(xmp) + f(xmm)) / (4 * eps**2)
            H[j, i] = H[i, j]
    return H

text:
MNL via Bayesian Estimation
We now fit the same MNL model using Bayesian methods, following the week-7 slides on Bayes’ rule and the random-walk Metropolis-Hastings sampler. The posterior is proportional to the likelihood times the prior:
\[
\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta} \mid \boldsymbol{y}) \propto L(\boldsymbol{\beta}) \cdot \pi(\boldsymbol{\beta})
\]
We use a weakly informative multivariate normal prior: \(\boldsymbol{\beta} \sim N(\mathbf{0},\; 10 \cdot I)\). With a standard deviation of approximately 3.2 on each \(\beta\), the prior covers a very wide range of utilities and places almost no constraint on the data.

def log_prior(beta_9):
    return np.sum(-0.5 * beta_9**2 / 10.0)

def log_posterior(beta_9):
    return log_likelihood(beta_9) + log_prior(beta_9)

def mh_sampler(beta0, n_iter, step, seed=42):
    np.random.seed(seed)
    K      = len(beta0)
    draws  = np.zeros((n_iter, K))
    beta   = beta0.copy()
    lp     = log_posterior(beta)
    accept = 0
    for t in range(n_iter):
        beta_star = beta + np.random.normal(0, step, K)
        lp_star   = log_posterior(beta_star)
        if np.log(np.random.uniform()) < lp_star - lp:
            beta = beta_star
            lp   = lp_star
            accept += 1
        draws[t] = beta
    return draws, accept / n_iter

Where all three methods agree. The rankings are identical across all three methods — every course occupies the same position whether we use counts, MLE, or Bayesian estimation. The top and bottom are especially stable: Mktg Analytics (495) leads by a wide margin in every method, and Consulting (444) is last in all three. This level of consistency reflects a dataset where the preference signal is strong relative to the noise.
Where they might disagree (and why). With a weaker signal — fewer respondents, fewer tasks, or items with more similar utilities — we would expect the middle of the ranking (roughly ranks 4–7) to shuffle across methods. In this dataset, Capstone (454), SQL (464), and Large Data (452) have fairly similar utilities, and a smaller sample might reorder them differently.
What MNL adds over counts. MNL uses the full choice-set structure: each best and worst decision is evaluated relative to the other items that appeared on the same screen. Counts uses exposure-adjusted summaries, but it does not model the probability of choosing one item over the specific alternatives shown in that task. This makes MNL statistically more efficient and produces preference shares with a natural probability interpretation, along with standard errors that support hypothesis testing.
What Bayes adds over MLE. The key advantage of the Bayesian approach is that uncertainty on derived quantities like preference shares is immediately available: for each MCMC draw, compute the softmax transformation and take percentiles across draws. Doing the same thing from MLE requires the delta method, which is approximate and more complex to implement. Bayesian estimation also extends naturally to hierarchical models that estimate individual-level preferences — a straightforward extension that is considerably harder to achieve with MLE.

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
Discussion
Substantive findings. Students in this MSBA cohort most strongly prefer Mktg Analytics (495), which receives a preference share of roughly 28% — nearly three times the equal-share benchmark of 10%. Biz Analytics (453, ≈11.7%) and Customer Analytics (455, ≈10.7%) follow in second and third. The common thread among the top-ranked courses is a focus on applied data analysis with direct business relevance. At the other end, Consulting (444) is the least preferred course by a clear margin, scoring below all others across all three methods. Mktg/Fin/Ops (451) and AI Math (403) also rank near the bottom.
One notable finding is SQL (464). Despite being one of the most practically valued skills in the job market, it lands in sixth place with a near-zero counts score. This may reflect a perception among MSBA students that SQL is a necessary baseline rather than a differentiating course — they may feel they already know it or can learn it independently, and so it neither excites nor deters them relative to more specialized offerings.
Methodological takeaways. The three approaches serve different purposes:

Counts is the right tool for a quick descriptive summary. It requires no modeling assumptions, is easy to communicate to a non-technical audience, and produces a result any manager can act on immediately.
MLE MNL is appropriate when rigorous point estimates with classical standard errors are needed — for example, when reporting to a committee that expects confidence intervals or significance tests.
Bayesian MNL is the best choice when uncertainty on derived quantities (preference shares, market-share simulations, “what if we added a new course?” scenarios) is important, or when the ultimate goal is a hierarchical model that estimates individual-level preferences and accounts for heterogeneity across students.

Caveats. The survey was administered to a self-selected sample of MSBA students, so results may not generalize to future cohorts or other programs. Preferences are likely influenced by factors not captured here: which courses a student has already completed, their academic background (engineering vs. business), and where they are in the program. MaxDiff also measures only relative preferences — it cannot detect a situation where all courses are uniformly liked or disliked.
Next steps. If time allowed, the most valuable extension would be a Hierarchical Bayes MNL that estimates a separate \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) vector for each respondent, drawn from a population-level distribution. This would reveal whether student preferences are homogeneous or whether meaningful subgroups exist — information that would be directly useful for advising, course scheduling, and curriculum design.
